2.text: The apparent difference which exists between the wind systems of the

3.text: peninsula and of the Kolyma country can be explained, to a considerable

4.text: degree, by the different position of land and sea in the two countries. Thus,

5.text: the sea-winds (añqaiˊhɪt) which on the Arctic Sea come from the north, on

6.text: the Pacific come from the east. Near the mouth of Kolyma River the wind

7.text: qêraˊlhɪn comes from the large open tundra of the west: on the Pacific, near

8.text: Indian Point, it is of the same nature, but comes from the southwest. The

9.text: wind qaačhêˊhɪn, which, near the mouth of Kolyma River, comes along the

10.text: seashore from the northeast, on the Pacific, near Indian Point, also comes

11.text: along the seashore, but from west-southwest.

12.text: The Koryak names of winds as diagrammed for me in the village of Vaˊikenan, on Penshina

13.text: Bay, are for the most part identical with those of the Pacific-coast Chukchee. Thus, qeyaˊlhɪn,

14.text: corresponding to the Chukchee qêraˊlhɪn, signifies “southwest;” eñeˊneñe signifies “southeast;” but

15.text: empeiˊkɪn, probably corresponding to yamwaˊihɪn of the Kolyma, which refers to the same wind,

17.text: Other winds among the Koryak of that village are hɪshoˊlan (“up-[stream wind]”) for the east
